name: Limit
definition: Describes the value a function approaches as its input approaches some point. The function need not attain the limit there; behavior nearby is what counts.
reading: “the limit as x approaches a of f of x”.

examples.explanation: x² gets arbitrarily close to 4 near x = 2.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Derivative (Lagrange notation)
definition: Gives the instantaneous rate of change of f at x: the slope of the tangent line. It is itself a function, the limit of average rates over shrinking intervals.

examples.explanation: At x = 3 the graph climbs with slope 6.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Derivative (Leibniz notation)
definition: Writes the derivative as a ratio of differentials: the change in y per change in x. It keeps the variable visible, which helps with the chain rule and related rates.

examples.explanation: Same derivative as f′(x), with the variable shown.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Partial derivative
definition: Differentiates a function of several variables with respect to one of them, holding the others fixed. The rounded ∂ distinguishes it from the ordinary d.
reading: “partial of f with respect to x”.

examples.tex: f(x, y) = x^2 y \Rightarrow \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2xy
examples.explanation: Treat y as a constant and differentiate in x.

commonMistakes: Reading ∂ as a Greek delta; it is a distinct symbol for partial change.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Differential
definition: Denotes an infinitesimal change in a variable. Differentials appear in integrals (dx marks the variable), in derivative ratios, and in linear approximations dy ≈ f′(x)dx.

examples.explanation: For y = x², a small step dx changes y by about 2x·dx.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Integral
definition: Accumulates a quantity: area under a curve, total from a rate, or an antiderivative. A definite integral carries limits and evaluates to a number; an indefinite one carries +C and gives a family of functions.
reading: “the integral of f of x d x”.

examples.explanation: Differentiating x³/3 returns x², so it is an antiderivative.
The triangular area under y = x from 0 to 1.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Double integral
definition: Integrates a function of two variables over a region: volume under a surface, or mass from a density. It is usually evaluated as two nested single integrals.
reading: “the double integral over R of f”.

examples.explanation: Integrating 1 over R gives the area of R.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Triple integral
definition: Integrates a function of three variables over a solid: hypervolume, or mass from a 3D density. Evaluated as three nested single integrals.
reading: “the triple integral over E of f”.

examples.explanation: Integrating 1 over E gives the volume of E.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Line integral
definition: Integrates along a curve C rather than an interval: work done by a force field, or total of a scalar field along a path.

examples.explanation: Work of the force field F along path C.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Contour (closed-loop) integral
definition: A line integral around a closed loop, marked by the circle on the integral sign. It measures circulation of a field or, in complex analysis, picks up enclosed singularities.

examples.explanation: Net circulation of F around the loop C.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Nabla (gradient)
definition: The vector differential operator (∂/∂x, ∂/∂y, ∂/∂z). Applied to a scalar field it gives the gradient: the direction and rate of steepest increase.

examples.explanation: Gradient of a two-variable function.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Divergence
definition: Measures how much a vector field spreads out from each point: positive divergence marks a source, negative a sink. It is a scalar built from partial derivatives.

examples.explanation: The field flows outward everywhere at rate 2.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Curl
definition: Measures the rotation of a vector field at each point: the axis and strength a paddle wheel would spin. Zero curl means locally rotation-free.

examples.explanation: Uniform counterclockwise rotation about the z-axis.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Laplacian
definition: The divergence of the gradient: the sum of unmixed second partials. It measures how a value differs from its local average, and appears in heat, wave and potential equations.

examples.explanation: Laplacian in two variables.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Epsilon-delta definition
definition: Makes “approaches” precise: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means every error tolerance ε around L can be met by keeping x within some distance δ of a.
reading: “for every epsilon there exists a delta”.

examples.explanation: Closeness in output is guaranteed by closeness in input.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Infinity
definition: Denotes unboundedness: growth beyond any bound, or a limit taken arbitrarily far out. It is not a number, so it follows special arithmetic rules.

examples.explanation: One over x vanishes as x grows without bound.
All nonnegative numbers; infinity takes a parenthesis.

commonMistakes: Treating ∞ − ∞ as 0; it is indeterminate without further analysis.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Supremum
definition: The least upper bound of a set: no member exceeds it, and any smaller number is exceeded by some member. It need not belong to the set.

examples.explanation: Nothing in the open interval reaches 1, yet nothing smaller bounds it.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Infimum
definition: The greatest lower bound of a set: no member goes below it, and any larger number is undercut by some member.

examples.explanation: Zero bounds the interval below without belonging to it.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Euler's number
definition: The base of natural logarithms, about 2.71828. It arises from continuous growth and has the defining property that eˣ is its own derivative.

examples.explanation: The compound-interest limit defining e.
Euler's identity links e, i, pi, 1 and 0.

sources.label: OpenStax Precalculus 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 4
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Riemann sum
definition: Approximates an integral by rectangles: sample the function in each subinterval, multiply by the width, and add. Finer subdivisions give better approximations; the limit is the integral.
reading: “the sum of f of x-i times delta x”.

examples.explanation: As rectangles narrow, the sum tends to the integral.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Continuity
definition: A function is continuous at a point when its limit there equals its value: no jump, break or hole. Polynomials, exponentials, sines and cosines are continuous everywhere they are defined.

examples.explanation: The three-part test: defined, limit exists, and they agree.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

notes: Continuity has no single standard symbol; the entry covers the concept because limits and derivatives depend on it.

name: L'Hôpital's rule
definition: For 0/0 or ∞/∞ limits with f and g differentiable near c (and g′ nonzero there), the limit of f/g equals the limit of f′/g′ when the latter exists. Confirm the indeterminate form first; the rule never applies otherwise.

examples.explanation: Both top and bottom vanish at 0, so differentiate each: cosine at 0 is 1.

commonMistakes: Applying the rule to a limit that is not 0/0 or ∞/∞.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Chain rule
definition: Differentiates a composition: differentiate the outer function evaluated at the inner value, then multiply by the inner function's derivative.
reading: “d y by d x equals d y by d u times d u by d x”.

examples.explanation: Outer derivative 2(3x+1) times inner derivative 3.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Integration by parts
definition: Integrates products by shifting the derivative: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Pick u to simplify under differentiation (logarithms, powers) and dv to integrate easily (exponentials, sines).

examples.tex: \int x e^x\,dx = x e^x - e^x + C
examples.explanation: With u = x and dv = e^x dx: uv minus the integral of v du.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 2
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Taylor series
definition: Rebuilds a smooth function from its derivatives at one point: matching value, slope, curvature and beyond. Centered at zero it is called a Maclaurin series; stopping after finitely many terms gives polynomial approximations.
reading: “the Taylor series of f at a”.

examples.explanation: Every derivative of eˣ at zero is 1, leaving the cleanest series of all.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 2
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
definition: Links differentiation and integration in two parts: differentiating an accumulated area recovers the function, and a definite integral equals any antiderivative's net change. It turns area problems into antiderivative evaluations.

examples.explanation: An antiderivative is x²; evaluate at the endpoints and subtract.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Mean value theorem
definition: On a smooth interval, the average slope is attained somewhere inside: some c has f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). It needs continuity on the closed interval and differentiability inside; Rolle's theorem is the flat case.

examples.explanation: Average slope 2 is attained at c = 1, inside the interval.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Improper integral
definition: An integral over an unbounded interval or of an unbounded function, defined as a limit of proper integrals. It converges when the limit exists finitely — infinite reach does not imply infinite area.

examples.explanation: Truncating at b gives 1 − 1/b, which tends to 1: finite area under an endless tail.

commonMistakes: Assuming an infinite interval always gives infinity; convergence must be checked.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 2
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Metric space
definition: A set equipped with a distance function d satisfying: distances are nonnegative, zero only for identical points, symmetric, and obey the triangle inequality d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,z). Metrics turn sets into geometric spaces where convergence makes sense.

examples.explanation: The usual distance on the real line; all four axioms are elementary absolute-value facts.

sources.label: UBC Real Analysis notes, metric completeness (Rechnitzer/Martens)
sources.license: Author/university course notes; consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Cauchy sequence
definition: A sequence whose terms get arbitrarily close to each other: for every ε > 0, all sufficiently late terms lie within ε. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy; a space is complete when the converse holds and every Cauchy sequence has its limit inside.

examples.explanation: Terms cluster together, but the limit 0 is missing from (0,1): Cauchy without converging there, so (0,1) is incomplete.

sources.label: UBC Real Analysis notes, metric completeness (Rechnitzer/Martens)
sources.license: Author/university course notes; consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Ordinary differential equation
definition: An equation for an unknown function of one variable involving its derivatives. The order is the highest derivative present; linear means y and its derivatives appear only to the first power, unmultiplied together.

examples.explanation: Differentiating Ce^{kt} gives kCe^{kt}: exponential growth (k > 0) or decay.

sources.label: LibreTexts, Differential Equation Terminology (Huber, IVC)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (page footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Partial differential equation
definition: An equation for an unknown function of several variables involving partial derivatives. The heat, wave, and Laplace equations are the canonical examples; boundary conditions pick the physical solution.

examples.explanation: The heat equation: temperature u spreads with diffusivity α.

sources.label: LibreTexts, Differential Equation Terminology (Huber, IVC)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (page footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Initial value problem
definition: A differential equation plus conditions fixing the solution's value (and derivatives, for higher order) at a point. An nth-order equation needs n conditions; with them, well-behaved problems have exactly one solution.

examples.explanation: General solution Ceˣ with C = 2 from y(0) = 2; check: (2eˣ)′ = 2eˣ.

sources.label: LibreTexts, Differential Equation Terminology (Huber, IVC)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (page footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Equilibrium and stability
definition: Constant solutions where the rate vanishes (y′ = 0). An equilibrium is stable when nearby solutions approach it and unstable when they move away — read off from the sign of the rate around it.

examples.explanation: Logistic growth: y = 1 attracts nearby solutions (stable); y = 0 repels them (unstable).

sources.label: LibreTexts, Differential Equation Terminology (Huber, IVC)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (page footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Lagrange multipliers
definition: Finds extrema of f subject to g = c: at the optimum the gradients align, ∇f = λ∇g, so level curves kiss the constraint. Solve this system jointly with the constraint itself.

examples.explanation: (1,1) = λ(2x,2y) gives x = y = 1/√2, value √2: the support line touches the circle.

sources.label: OpenStax Calculus Volume 3
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Convex function
definition: A function whose chord always lies above its graph (f″ ≥ 0 where twice differentiable): it cups upward, so any local minimum is global. Flipping the inequality gives concave.

examples.explanation: Second derivative 2 > 0 everywhere: every tangent sits below the parabola.
